prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks that measure time with unprecedented precision

statement.case_for: Having read the other seven ballots, I move my preferred configuration from the baryon acoustic oscillation ballot (B016, my opening first place) to the optical lattice clock (B019). The discovery is a measurement capability that opens a new way of observing nature: the magic-wavelength idea (Katori) removes the light shift from the lattice, and the Ye group's strontium work took the instrument to the 1e-18 level, where one sees the gravitational redshift across a millimetre and can test the constancy of constants. That is exactly the kind of clue from nature I want a prize to reward, and the discovery is clearly delineated, with a natural two-person attribution. Three colleagues (Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce) place it first and Olsson and Mehlig also rank it, so it is the broadest consensus on the table. It is mature, reproduced at JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST, and the redefinition of the second makes recognition timely.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that it sits close to earlier metrology prizes (the 2005 frequency comb, the 2012 ion-trap prize, and laser cooling in 1997 and 2018), so it may look like the next increment in a well-honoured line rather than a new discovery. Credit is also shared with other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Gill, Peik on ion clocks, and the many JILA co-workers), and the committee must be sure that Katori and Ye are the right pair. Finally, my own opening favourite, BAO, is arguably more directly about the content of the universe, and I should not let the fact that I find dark energy personally interesting inflate its standing.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a decisive step in measurement precision, underpinning relativistic geodesy, constant tests and the redefinition of the second, with a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree on the discovery and the pair, and this is what moved me. I would add one qualification to the argument from the redefinition of the second: that is an application of the metrology community's consensus, and the prize should rest on the physics (the magic-wavelength trapping and the 1e-18 systematics), not on a pending SI decision. I would write the citation around the clock as an instrument, not the second.

responses.point: Mehlig puts active-matter hydrodynamics (Vicsek, Toner, Ramaswamy) first as a universal non-equilibrium mechanism, and ranks lattice clocks only sixth because of closeness to earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: I take the metrology-overlap point seriously and listed it as my main reservation, but the frequency comb was about a tool for spectroscopy and the lattice clock is a different discovery. On B009 I respect the conceptual elegance, but only one member ranks it, the credited trio lacks Yuhai Tu who is central to the Toner-Tu theory, and I would want the committee to commission an outside evaluation before moving it forward. I disagree that it should lead this year.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because theory told the community where to look and the 2018 experiments found correlated and superconducting states.
responses.response: I find the theory-plus-experiment story strong, and B047 is one of my two alternatives. But I side with Eriksson and Johansson's caution on maturity: eight years in, nobody agrees on why it superconducts, and the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi and others are not in the names) is the weakest part of the attribution. I would rather wait than prize a field whose central interpretation is still moving.

responses.point: Pearce ranks lattice clocks first as patient calibration-and-systematics work, and ranks BAO fourth, noting the credit is shared between SDSS and 2dFGRS and the theory predates 2005.
responses.response: I accept the fair criticism of my own opening choice: the BAO credit is spread across two survey collaborations with earlier theory (Peebles and Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich) outside the names, and the DESI hints of evolving dark energy are still open. I still think BAO is a worthy discovery and keep it as an alternative, but I agree that the clock is the cleaner attribution this year.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the physics of strong light-matter coupling and the basis of superconducting qubits, following naturally on the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I think the argument from the 2025 prize cuts the other way: a physics prize on superconducting circuits has just been awarded and committee practice normally avoids returning to the same platform so quickly, even if circuit QED is a distinct discovery. I also doubt the attribution, since Girvin, Devoret and the transmon work at Yale blur a clean three-person credit. It is a strong ballot but I would not put it ahead of the clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to reward a third metrology-adjacent prize within two decades, and whether outside experts see lattice clocks as a new discovery rather than a continuation.
Whether Katori and Ye are the whole story, given contributions from Lemonde, Derevianko and other lattice-clock groups.
How much weight to give BAO now that DESI results suggest evolving dark energy, which could strengthen or complicate the case.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will look more or less mature after a few more years of work on the superconducting mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My PhD supervisor (Gross), my mentor (Rubinstein) and my co-author (Van Riet) are not connected to any shortlisted candidate, but I declare that my own research interest in dark energy may bias me toward B016.
